model.name: Binding minimum wage in a competitive labour market for security guards
model.status: illustrative: invented schedules generated from declared linear equations; example rates, not Namibia's legal minimum wage
assumptions: Basic competitive labour market: many employers, none able to set the wage alone.
The minimum wage is above the equilibrium wage, so it is binding; a floor below N$25 would have no effect.
The floor does not shift labour demand or labour supply; employment equals labour demanded at the floor.
The result is specific to this model; it is not a claim that every minimum wage reduces employment.

question.title: Competitive labour market for security guards before a minimum wage
question.description: Labour demand curve D and labour supply curve S for security guards, with wage (N$ per hour) vertically and quantity of labour (guards) horizontally. Text states that the government sets a minimum wage of N$30 an hour.

text: The government sets a minimum wage

answer.title: Binding minimum wage creates an excess supply of labour in the competitive model
answer.description: Original equilibrium E at N$25 an hour and 400 guards. A minimum wage of N$30, above equilibrium, is drawn as a horizontal line. Neither curve shifts: at N$30 firms want 300 guards (on D) and 500 people want to work (on S), an excess supply of labour of 200. In this model employment falls from 400 to 300.

text: At the N$30 minimum wage: firms want 300, 500 want work
In this competitive model, employment falls 400 to 300
